set.detail:
In the spring of 312 Constantine crossed the Alps by the Mont Genèvre or Mont Cenis with perhaps 40,000 men, a quarter of his army, leaving the rest to guard the Rhine. He stormed Segusio, defeated Maxentius' heavy cavalry (clibanarii) near Turin by letting their charge pass through opened ranks and clubbing the armoured riders from their horses, entered Milan, won at Brescia, besieged and took Verona after killing Maxentius' praetorian prefect Ruricius Pompeianus in a hard battle, and then marched on Rome. Zosimus gives Maxentius 188,000 men, wildly inflated, but he certainly outnumbered Constantine and could have sat out a siege behind the Aurelian Walls, which he had raised and supplied.

Instead, Lactantius says, after riots in the Circus in which the crowd chanted that Constantine was invincible, Maxentius consulted the Sibylline Books, which declared that 'on this day the enemy of the Romans will perish'. On 28 October 312, the sixth anniversary of his accession, he crossed the Tiber on a bridge of boats beside the partly demolished Milvian Bridge and drew up on the plain near Saxa Rubra with the river behind him. Constantine's Gallic cavalry broke Maxentius' horse on the wings; the Praetorians fought and died where they stood; the rest fled back to the bridge of boats, which collapsed under them. Maxentius drowned in the Tiber with many of his men. His body was recovered and his head carried on a spear into Rome the next day, then sent to Africa.

Constantine entered Rome on 29 October, disbanded the Praetorian Guard and its horse guard, the equites singulares, and was hailed by the Senate as senior Augustus. Eusebius compared the drowning to Pharaoh's army in the Red Sea. The battle made Constantine master of the west and, through the vision that preceded it and the Christian sign on his soldiers' shields, became the founding moment of the Christian empire. The Arch of Constantine (315) shows the battle with Maxentius' men drowning.

scholarship: Barnes, Constantine (2011)
Van Dam, Remembering Constantine at the Milvian Bridge (2011)

set.detail:
The late Roman army differed sharply from that of the Principate, and ancient and modern writers credit Constantine with key steps. After 312 he abolished the Praetorian Guard and the equites singulares and relied on new mounted guard units, the scholae palatinae, under the master of offices. He built up a large mobile army attached to the emperor's person, the comitatus, whose soldiers (comitatenses) enjoyed better pay and privileges than the frontier troops, known first as ripenses and later limitanei; a law of 325 (CTh 7.20.4) already distinguishes comitatenses, ripenses and auxiliaries. New infantry units, the auxilia palatina such as the Cornuti and Brachiati, many recruited among Germans, became the elite of the field army, while the legions were reduced to units of about 1,000 men.

Command was reorganised. Constantine created the posts of magister peditum and magister equitum, the masters of foot and horse, who took over the military functions of the praetorian prefects; the prefects became purely civil officials in charge of supply, finance and justice in regional prefectures. Frontier troops were placed under duces in each sector. Germanic officers rose to the top: Bonitus, father of Silvanus, under Constantine, then Magnentius, Silvanus and many others.

Zosimus, a hostile pagan writing c. 500, accused Constantine of ruining the empire by withdrawing troops from the frontiers into cities where they grew soft, leaving the borders exposed. Modern debate concerns whether Diocletian or Constantine created the field army: Jones and van Berchem stressed Diocletian's increase of the frontier forces and the comitatus, while others (Nicasie, Southern and Dixon) see a gradual evolution from Gallienus' cavalry to Constantine's comitatenses. The system was later formalised into regional field armies, as shown in the Notitia Dignitatum around 400.

scholarship: Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964)
Nicasie, Twilight of Empire: The Roman Army from the Reign of Diocletian until the Battle of Adrianople (1998)
Southern and Dixon, The Late Roman Army (1996)

set.detail:
Two versions of Constantine's conversion experience survive. Lactantius, writing about 314-315 in De Mortibus Persecutorum, says that on the night before the battle at the Milvian Bridge Constantine was told in a dream to mark 'the heavenly sign of God' on his soldiers' shields, and did so by drawing 'the letter X turned, with its top bent around', most likely a staurogram or a chi-rho. Eusebius of Caesarea, in the Life of Constantine written after the emperor's death in 337, tells a different story that he claims to have heard from Constantine himself on oath: while marching with his army earlier in the campaign, at midday, Constantine and all his soldiers saw a cross of light above the sun with the words 'By this conquer' (Greek touto nika; Latin in hoc signo vinces). That night Christ appeared to him in a dream with the same sign and told him to make a likeness of it as a protection in battle. Eusebius then describes the labarum, a tall gilded spear with a crossbar and a wreath enclosing the chi-rho, from which hung a square banner with portraits of the emperor and his sons.

Earlier, in 310, a panegyrist reported that Constantine had seen Apollo with Victory at a shrine in Gaul (probably Grand), offering him laurel wreaths with the numeral XXX. Peter Weiss proposed that Constantine saw a solar halo phenomenon in 310, interpreted first in pagan and later in Christian terms. The chi-rho appears on a silver medallion of Ticinum around 315 on Constantine's helmet, while Sol Invictus remained on his coins until about 322.

The debate is endless: was the conversion a sudden experience (Barnes), a gradual shift from solar monotheism (Bleckmann, Van Dam), or political calculation? What is clear is that from 312 Constantine identified his victories with the Christian God and lavished favours on the church.

scholarship: Weiss, "The Vision of Constantine", JRA 16 (2003)
Barnes, Constantine (2011)
Bleckmann, Konstantin der Grosse (1996)

set.detail:
In February 313 Constantine and Licinius met at Milan, where Licinius married Constantine's half-sister Constantia. They agreed a common religious policy. No edict as such survives, and the familiar title is a modern convention criticised since Otto Seeck. What we have is a letter issued by Licinius after his victory over Maximinus Daia at Tzirallum (30 April 313), posted at Nicomedia on 13 June 313 and preserved in Latin by Lactantius, and a Greek version addressed to the governor of Palestine in Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History.

The text states that 'when I, Constantine Augustus, and I, Licinius Augustus, met happily at Milan', they decided to grant 'both to Christians and to all others free power to follow the religion each wished', so that 'whatever divinity there is in heaven may be favourable to us and all under our rule'. All restrictions on Christians were removed; meeting places and other property confiscated from Christians, including those belonging to the Christian community as a corporate body, were to be returned at once without payment, and those who had bought or received them as gifts could seek compensation from the treasury.

In the west Constantine had already, after the Milvian Bridge, ordered restitution of church property in Africa and exempted clergy from civic duties (letters to Anullinus). The Milan agreement extended these measures to the east once Licinius defeated Maximinus. Its importance lies in the principle of religious liberty for all and the recognition of the church as a legal body able to own property, which made possible the church's growth into a wealthy institution. Modern scholars stress that it was not the establishment of Christianity as the state religion, which took decades, and that Licinius soon turned against the church.

scholarship: Seeck, "Das sogenannte Edikt von Mailand", ZKG 12 (1891)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)

set.detail:
Arius, a Libyan-born ascetic presbyter in charge of the church of Baucalis in Alexandria, taught around 318 (the date is disputed, some prefer 320-322) that God the Father alone was without beginning and that the Son, though created before all ages and through him all things, was created out of nothing by the Father's will. 'There was when he was not', 'before he was begotten, he was not', and the Son was 'not equal to the Father' became the slogans of his opponents' summaries. He drew on a subordinationist reading of Origen and on biblical texts such as Proverbs 8:22 ('the Lord created me at the beginning of his ways'). His Thalia, a work partly in verse, was popular; Philostorgius says he wrote songs for sailors, millers and travellers.

Bishop Alexander of Alexandria, insisting on the Son's eternal generation, condemned Arius at a synod of about a hundred Egyptian and Libyan bishops and excommunicated him with several presbyters and deacons. Arius found support from his fellow pupils of Lucian of Antioch, the 'Collucianists', especially the powerful Eusebius of Nicomedia, and from Eusebius of Caesarea; synods in Bithynia and Palestine backed him. A war of encyclical letters followed, which Alexander circulated widely. After defeating Licinius in 324, Constantine sent Ossius of Cordoba with a letter describing the dispute as a trivial question of words, but reconciliation failed; a synod at Antioch early in 325 condemned Arius' supporters, and the emperor called the council of Nicaea.

Modern scholars (Hanson, Rowan Williams, Gwynn) emphasise that 'Arianism' as a coherent heresy is largely a construct of Athanasius' polemic; the following decades saw a spectrum of positions (homoians, homoiousians, anomoeans) rather than an Arian party loyal to Arius. The controversy dominated church politics for sixty years until the council of Constantinople in 381, and among the Goths and other Germanic peoples into the sixth century.

scholarship: Hanson, The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God (1988)
Williams, Arius: Heresy and Tradition (2nd ed., 2001)
Gwynn, The Eusebians (2007)

set.detail:
The final war between Constantine and Licinius began in 324 after years of tension, Constantine's incursion into Licinius' Thrace while pursuing Goths in 323, and Licinius' restrictions on Christians. On 3 July 324 Constantine defeated Licinius at Adrianople, and his son Crispus destroyed Licinius' fleet under Abantus (Amandus) at the Hellespont, opening the straits. Licinius abandoned Byzantium, crossed to Asia and proclaimed his master of offices Martinianus as co-Augustus.

Constantine ferried his army across the Bosporus in light vessels and on 18 September 324 attacked Licinius' army near Chrysopolis (Üsküdar), on the Asian shore opposite Byzantium. Licinius' forces included Gothic auxiliaries under their chief Alica. Eusebius emphasises the protective power of the labarum, carried by a picked guard to wherever the line wavered. The battle was a crushing victory: Zosimus speaks of some 25,000 Licinian dead and the rest scattering. Licinius fled to Nicomedia with about 30,000 survivors and, after his wife Constantia interceded with her brother, surrendered on the promise of his life. He was sent to live as a private citizen at Thessalonica with Martinianus, but both were executed in 325 on the charge, perhaps fabricated, of plotting with the Goths.

Chrysopolis left Constantine the sole ruler of the empire, the first since 285 (and the last until Theodosius briefly in 394-395). Within weeks he founded Constantinople on the site of Byzantium as a victory city, raised his son Constantius to Caesar (8 November 324) and extended his pro-Christian policies to the east, summoning the council of Nicaea for 325. Christian writers presented the war as a crusade; modern historians see it as a power struggle in which religion was an instrument of propaganda.

scholarship: Odahl, Constantine and the Christian Empire (2004)
Barnes, Constantine (2011)

set.detail:
Immediately after Chrysopolis, on 8 November 324, Constantine marked out the boundaries of a new city on the site of Byzantium, the Greek colony on the promontory between the Golden Horn, the Bosporus and the Sea of Marmara, which Septimius Severus had punished in 196 and then rebuilt. Philostorgius tells that the emperor walked the line on foot, spear in hand, and when his companions asked how far he would go, replied, 'Until he who walks before me stops'. The new land wall ran about 2.8 km west of the Severan wall, roughly quadrupling the area of the city to about six square kilometres. On the same day he made his son Constantius Caesar.

The city was built rapidly. Its main features were the Mese (main street), the round Forum of Constantine with a porphyry column topped by a statue of the emperor as Apollo-Helios, the enlarged Hippodrome linked to the Great Palace, the Augustaion, a Senate house, the baths of Zeuxippus and the church of the Holy Apostles, designed as Constantine's mausoleum. Statues were taken from all over the eastern Mediterranean, including the Serpent Column from Delphi, set up on the spina of the Hippodrome; Jerome remarked that Constantinople was dedicated by stripping nearly every other city bare. Settlers were attracted by the grant of houses and from 332 by a free bread dole on the Roman model, said to be 80,000 rations. A senate was created, initially of lower rank than Rome's.

Why Constantine chose Byzantium remains debated: strategic location between the Danube and Euphrates fronts and at a nodal point of land and sea routes, a victory monument, and a Christian capital free of Rome's pagan traditions have all been proposed. Gilbert Dagron's Naissance d'une capitale argues that it became 'New Rome' only gradually, under Constantius II and Theodosius I, from one imperial residence among several to the capital of the east.

scholarship: Dagron, Naissance d'une capitale: Constantinople et ses institutions de 330 à 451 (1974)
Mango, Le développement urbain de Constantinople (1985)

set.detail:
Constantine originally summoned the council to Ancyra but moved it to Nicaea in Bithynia, closer to his residence at Nicomedia, offering bishops free use of the imperial post. It opened around 20 May 325 (some sources give 19 June) in the imperial palace, with between 250 and 300 bishops; later tradition fixed the number at 318, the servants of Abraham. Almost all came from the eastern provinces; the west was represented by Ossius of Cordoba, two Roman presbyters (Vitus and Vincentius) for the aged Pope Silvester, Caecilian of Carthage and a handful of others. Constantine entered in purple and gold, addressed the bishops in Latin and took part in the debates.

No minutes survive. From Eusebius' letter to his church, Athanasius' On the Decrees of Nicaea and the church historians, we know that the council condemned Arius and adopted a creed declaring the Son 'begotten, not made, of one substance (homoousios) with the Father', with anathemas against those who said 'there was when he was not' or that the Son was of another hypostasis or ousia. The term homoousios, possibly suggested by Constantine or Ossius, was accepted by Eusebius of Caesarea with reservations. Arius and two Libyan bishops who refused to sign were exiled to Illyricum, and Eusebius of Nicomedia and Theognis of Nicaea soon after. The council also settled the Melitian schism, agreed that Easter should be celebrated on the same Sunday everywhere without reference to Jewish calculations, and issued twenty canons, including canon 6 recognising the authority of Alexandria over Egypt, Libya and the Pentapolis on the model of Rome, and canon 7 honouring Jerusalem. The council closed with a banquet for Constantine's vicennalia in late July.

Nicaea became the first 'ecumenical council', but its creed only achieved its central place after 350 thanks to Athanasius and the Cappadocians; for decades many bishops preferred other formulas. It established the model of the emperor convening and enforcing church councils.

scholarship: Ayres, Nicaea and Its Legacy (2004)
Kim (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Council of Nicaea (2021)

set.detail:
Shortly after Nicaea Constantine wrote to Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem, ordering the demolition of the temple of Venus that Hadrian had built over the site venerated by local Christians as Christ's tomb, and the construction of a basilica 'more beautiful than any in the world', funded by the imperial treasury and supplied with columns and marble by the governor of Palestine. Excavation uncovered a rock-cut tomb, which Eusebius describes as resurrection after burial. The complex, dedicated in 335, comprised the Anastasis rotunda over the tomb (completed later), a courtyard with the rock of Golgotha, and the five-aisled basilica of the Martyrium.

Constantine's mother Helena, now Augusta and nearly eighty, travelled through the eastern provinces to the Holy Land, probably in 326-328, a year after the executions of Crispus and Fausta in which she may have had a part. Eusebius says she prayed at the holy places, gave money to soldiers, cities and the poor, freed prisoners and founded churches at the cave of the Nativity in Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives (the Eleona) over the cave associated with the Ascension. She died soon after, probably in 329, and was buried in a porphyry sarcophagus (now in the Vatican Museums) in a mausoleum on the Via Labicana beside the church of Saints Marcellinus and Peter. Drepanum in Bithynia, her birthplace, was renamed Helenopolis.

Eusebius says nothing about the True Cross. The story of Helena discovering it, identified by a miracle, appears first in Ambrose's funeral oration for Theodosius in 395 and in Rufinus, and developed into one of the most influential legends of the Middle Ages. Modern scholars (Hunt, Drijvers) see Helena's journey as an imperial progress combining piety and politics, and the Holy Sepulchre as the beginning of the Christian 'holy land' and mass pilgrimage.

scholarship: Drijvers, Helena Augusta (1992)
Hunt, Holy Land Pilgrimage in the Later Roman Empire (1982)

set.detail:
On Monday 11 May 330 Constantine formally dedicated his new city, which bore his name. The Chronicon Paschale describes forty days of celebrations, races in the Hippodrome and distributions to the people. A gilded wooden statue of Constantine holding a small figure of the Tyche of the city was carried in procession into the Hippodrome, escorted by soldiers in white with candles, and the reigning emperor was to rise and bow to it each year on the city's birthday, a ceremony performed into the sixth century. The city's Tyche bore the name Anthousa ('flourishing'), possibly a Greek translation of the secret name of Rome, Flora.

Special coins were struck in all mints: CONSTANTINOPOLIS, with a helmeted personification and Victory on a ship's prow, and URBS ROMA, with the wolf and twins, presenting the two capitals as equals. Later Byzantine tradition claimed that pagan rites accompanied the foundation: that the philosopher Sopater, later executed, assisted, that the astrologer Vettius Valens cast its horoscope, and that the Palladium of Troy and Rome was buried under the porphyry column of Constantine's forum, along with Christian relics. Zosimus says Constantine built temples to Rhea and to the Tyche of Rome. Eusebius, in contrast, presents it as a Christian city free of idols, with fountains decorated with the Good Shepherd and Daniel.

The population grew fast; by the end of the century the city needed extensions and in the early fifth century Theodosius II built the great land walls further west. The dedication date became the anniversary of the empire that lasted until 1453, and 11 May was celebrated in the church calendar as the birthday of the city. Historians debate how far Constantine intended a new capital rather than a monumental imperial residence like Nicomedia or Trier.

scholarship: Dagron, Naissance d'une capitale (1974)
Bassett, The Urban Image of Late Antique Constantinople (2004)

set.detail:
In 336-337 Shapur II intervened in Armenia and Constantine prepared a great expedition against Persia, planning to be baptised in the Jordan and taking with him bishops and a tent-church. Around Easter 337 he fell ill in Constantinople. He went to the hot baths of Helenopolis in Bithynia and then to a villa called Achyron near Nicomedia, where, realising he was dying, he asked for baptism, which he had deferred, as was common, until the end of his life. Eusebius of Nicomedia, the leader of the anti-Athanasian bishops, baptised him; he then refused to wear the purple again, dressing only in white baptismal robes. He died at noon on the feast of Pentecost, 22 May 337, aged about 65, after nearly 31 years of rule.

The body was placed in a golden coffin and brought to the palace in Constantinople, where officials continued to do homage to it as if he were alive, while his sons were notified. Constantius arrived first and conducted the funeral; Constantine was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles, surrounded by twelve cenotaphs of the apostles, as if he were a thirteenth apostle, which later earned him the title isapostolos in Orthodox tradition. Coins showed him veiled and, on the reverse, ascending in a four-horse chariot towards the hand of God; the Senate in Rome deified him in traditional form, the last emperor to receive consecratio.

There was no Augustus for more than three months. During the summer the army in Constantinople murdered most of the male relatives of Constantine except his three sons, who took the title Augustus on 9 September 337. Eusebius' Life of Constantine, finished soon after, is a panegyric that shaped all later views of the first Christian emperor, while Julian and Zosimus portrayed him as a spendthrift innovator who ruined the empire.

scholarship: Barnes, Constantine (2011)
Johnson, The Roman Imperial Mausoleum in Late Antiquity (2009)

set.detail:
Constantine had arranged a power-sharing succession in 335 that included not only his three sons (Constantine II, Constantius II and Constans) but also his nephews Dalmatius, as Caesar with Thrace, Macedonia and Achaea, and Hannibalianus, as 'King of Kings and of the Pontic peoples' for Armenia, both sons of his half-brother Flavius Dalmatius, son of Constantius I and Theodora. After Constantine's death in May 337 the army in Constantinople declared it would accept no rulers but his sons. In the summer soldiers killed Constantine's half-brothers Julius Constantius and Flavius Dalmatius, the Caesar Dalmatius, Hannibalianus, the patrician Optatus and several others; the powerful praetorian prefect Ablabius was dismissed and killed soon afterwards. Only two young sons of Julius Constantius survived, Gallus, who was ill and expected to die, and the six-year-old Julian; both later became Caesars.

Responsibility was disputed from the start. Eusebius, writing immediately afterwards, presents the soldiers acting spontaneously out of loyalty to Constantine's sons. Philostorgius tells of a forged will claiming Constantine had been poisoned by his brothers. Julian, in his Letter to the Athenians (361), blames Constantius directly for the murder of his father, uncle and cousins, and Zosimus and other writers follow. Ammianus and Athanasius also hint at Constantius' guilt.

Richard Burgess, in 'The Summer of Blood' (2008), argues that Constantius, the only son present in Constantinople, orchestrated the killings to eliminate rivals and secure his share, with the agreement of his brothers, who met in Pannonia in 338 to divide the empire. The massacre shaped the psychology and politics of the dynasty: Julian's hatred of Constantius and his reaction against the Christianity of his cousin's court are inseparable from it, and the narrowing of the family made the dynasty fragile after Constans' and Constantius' deaths.

scholarship: Burgess, "The Summer of Blood: The 'Great Massacre' of 337 and the Promotion of the Sons of Constantine", DOP 62 (2008)

set.detail:
By 350 Constans, sole ruler of the west since the death of Constantine II in 340, had become unpopular with the army; Aurelius Victor and Zosimus accuse him of greed, favouring handsome barbarian bodyguards and neglecting the troops. On 18 January 350, at Augustodunum (Autun), the comes rei privatae Marcellinus held a birthday banquet for his son; late in the evening Flavius Magnentius, commander of two elite units (the Joviani and Herculiani), withdrew and reappeared in imperial purple, and the guests acclaimed him. Constans, hunting nearby, fled towards Spain but was caught and killed at Helena (Elne) at the foot of the Pyrenees by a party under Gaiso.

Magnentius was a professional soldier of barbarian descent; Zosimus says his father was a Briton and his mother a Frank, and Julian implies he had been a prisoner of war settled as a laetus. Gaul, Britain, Spain, Africa and Italy recognised him. In Rome Constans' cousin Nepotianus proclaimed himself on 3 June 350 with gladiators and the mob, but Magnentius' general Marcellinus killed him after 28 days and massacred his supporters. In Illyricum the old magister peditum Vetranio was proclaimed on 1 March 350, encouraged by Constantius' sister Constantina, perhaps to keep the Danube army from Magnentius; he abdicated to Constantius in a staged scene at Naissus on 25 December 350.

Magnentius made his brother Decentius Caesar and sought recognition, offering marriage alliances, but Constantius refused. His coinage is notable for the first large chi-rho with alpha and omega as the main reverse type, showing that he was a Christian, though Constantius later accused him of permitting pagan nocturnal sacrifices. The civil war that followed, culminating at Mursa (351) and Mons Seleucus (353), cost Rome tens of thousands of trained soldiers and opened the Rhine frontier to the Alamanni and Franks.

scholarship: Drinkwater, "The Revolt and Ethnic Origin of the Usurper Magnentius", Chiron 30 (2000)

set.detail:
After refusing negotiations, Constantius II advanced into Pannonia in 351. Magnentius, with an army of Gallic, Frankish and Saxon troops, took Siscia and struck at Sirmium, then turned against Constantius' army near Mursa (Osijek) on the Drava. On the eve of battle Magnentius' commander Silvanus deserted with his cavalry, a blow to the usurper. The battle was fought on 28 September 351 on the plain before Mursa and lasted until nightfall. Constantius' armoured cavalry, the clibanarii and cataphracts, and mounted archers broke Magnentius' left wing and outflanked his army; the Gallic infantry fought stubbornly until surrounded.

The casualties were enormous. Zonaras, probably drawing on a good source, says Constantius lost 30,000 of his 80,000 men and Magnentius 24,000 of 36,000. Eutropius says the battle consumed 'enormous forces of the empire, sufficient for any foreign war, which could have won many triumphs and secured peace'. Sulpicius Severus tells that Constantius waited out the battle in the martyrs' church outside the city with the Homoian bishop Valens of Mursa, who announced the victory before the messengers arrived, claiming an angel had told him, which won him the emperor's lasting favour. Magnentius fled to Aquileia and then to Gaul.

The victory decided the war: in 352 Constantius recovered Italy, and in 353 he defeated Magnentius at Mons Seleucus in the Cottian Alps, after which Magnentius killed himself at Lugdunum and Decentius at Sens. But the losses had strategic consequences. Many units of the western field army were destroyed or transferred east (Magnentian legions later fought at Amida), and Franks and Alamanni, some encouraged by Constantius against Magnentius, overran the Rhineland, sacking Cologne in 355. Julian's Gallic campaigns were the response. Mursa is often called the bloodiest battle of the fourth century.

scholarship: Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay (2014)
Barnes, Athanasius and Constantius (1993)

set.detail:
In August 357 an Alamannic coalition of seven kings led by Chnodomarius, a giant figure with a flame-coloured helmet, and his nephew Serapio, who had been given a Greek name by his father, a hostage in Gaul initiated in the mysteries, crossed the Rhine near Strasbourg. A deserter told Julian they numbered 35,000. The other half of the Roman pincer, Barbatio's 25,000, had been driven back near Augst. Julian, with about 13,000 men, marched from Saverne and found the enemy drawn up near Argentoratum in the afternoon. He wanted to camp and fight next day, but his officers and men insisted on battle.

Ammianus, who knew officers present, gives a detailed narrative. The Alamannic princes, at the demand of their warriors, dismounted to fight on foot. On the Roman right, the cataphracts broke and fled after their commander was wounded, but Julian rallied them in person, like Sulla, his standard of a purple dragon. In the centre the Alamannic warriors charged repeatedly against the shield wall; the auxilia palatina Cornuti and Brachiati, the Batavi and the Reges held, and when a body of nobles broke through the first line, the legion of the Primani in the second line stopped them. The Alamanni finally broke and fled to the Rhine, where many drowned under Roman missiles. Ammianus counts 6,000 Alamanni dead on the field and countless in the river, against 243 Roman dead and four officers, including Bainobaudes, tribune of the Cornuti, and Innocentius, commander of the cataphracts.

Chnodomarius was captured in a wood near the river and sent to Constantius, who claimed the victory in his own name; the king died in Rome in the camp of the Peregrini. The soldiers hailed Julian as Augustus, which he refused. The battle restored Roman control of the Rhine, allowed Julian to cross the river in 357-359 and impose treaties on the Alamannic kings, and made him a hero to the Gallic army.

scholarship: Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome 213-496 (2007)
Elton, Warfare in Roman Europe AD 350-425 (1996)

set.detail:
In 359 Shapur II, having secured his eastern frontier against the Chionites, who now joined him as allies under their king Grumbates, invaded Roman Mesopotamia with a large army including Albanians and Segestani, guided by the Roman defector Antoninus, a former merchant and accountant who had advised him to strike at the Euphrates crossings. The Roman commander Ursicinus, with his protector Ammianus Marcellinus, failed to stop the advance and Ammianus took refuge in Amida (Diyarbakır) on the upper Tigris. The city's normal garrison of legio V Parthica had been reinforced to seven legions, including two Gallic legions that had served Magnentius, and was crowded with refugees, giving it some 120,000 people within its basalt walls.

Shapur hoped to overawe Amida, but when Grumbates rode up to demand surrender his son was killed by a bolt from a ballista. The Persians besieged the city for 73 days. Ammianus, the only ancient historian who was inside a besieged city, describes a plague after ten days, the Gallic legions' night sortie that killed many Persians before they were driven back, a tower taken by 70 Persian archers who entered through a secret passage shown by a deserter, and mounds raised against the walls. Finally a Roman counter-mound collapsed and bridged the gap, and the Persians poured in. Ammianus escaped at night through a postern; the count Aelianus and the Gallic tribunes were crucified, and many inhabitants were killed or deported. The fall came in early October 359.

The siege cost Shapur heavily, 30,000 dead according to Ammianus' informant, and so much time that he could not advance further that year. It brought Constantius east and led to the demand for Julian's troops that provoked his usurpation in 360. Ammianus' account in books 18-19 is one of the great siege narratives of antiquity.

scholarship: Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)
Kelly, Ammianus Marcellinus: The Allusive Historian (2008)

set.detail:
In the winter of 359-360, facing the Persian offensive, Constantius ordered Julian to send east the four best auxiliary units of the Gallic army, the Heruli, Batavi, Celtae and Petulantes, plus 300 men from each of the other units, under the command of the tribune of the stable Sintula, with the notary Decentius to supervise. Many of the soldiers were Germans recruited from across the Rhine on the condition that they would never serve beyond the Alps; an anonymous pamphlet circulated in the camp complaining that they were being torn from their families. Julian, against advice, let the troops pass through Lutetia (Paris), his winter quarters, where they were entertained.

At night, in February or March 360, the soldiers surrounded the palace and hailed Julian as Augustus. He refused, then yielded; since he had no diadem, they suggested his wife Helena's necklace or a horse's ornament, until Maurus, a standard-bearer of the Petulantes, put his gold torque on Julian's head. Julian promised each man five gold pieces and a pound of silver. In his Letter to the Athenians he claims he prayed to Zeus for a sign and received one, and that the proclamation surprised him. He wrote to Constantius offering to remain Caesar in effect, sending troops and accepting a praetorian prefect from him, but Constantius refused, ordering him to be content with the rank of Caesar.

The relationship deteriorated into open war in 361: Julian marched east down the Danube, while Constantius prepared to march west from Antioch, when he died at Mopsucrenae on 3 November 361, naming Julian as his successor. Ammianus presents Julian as an unwilling candidate; Eunapius and modern scholars such as Bowersock suspect he engineered the mutiny, perhaps with his physician Oribasius, to escape Constantius' control.

scholarship: Bowersock, Julian the Apostate (1978)
Tougher, Julian the Apostate (2007)

set.detail:
Julian, raised as a Christian, had secretly returned to the gods around 351 under the influence of the Neoplatonist Maximus of Ephesus, a theurgist in the tradition of Iamblichus. Once sole emperor he declared himself openly. A decree early in 362 ordered temples reopened, sacrifices restored and temple property returned, which led to violence where churches had been built on temple land. He recalled all bishops exiled by Constantius, Nicenes and Homoians alike, so that, Ammianus says, their quarrels would weaken the church: 'no wild beasts are so hostile to men as most Christians are to one another'. Christians lost privileges and immunities, and the law on teachers of June 362 excluded them from teaching classical literature.

Julian tried to give paganism the structure and moral force he admired in the church. He appointed high priests for provinces, such as Theodorus in Asia and Arsacius in Galatia, and in letters urged them to live austerely, avoid the theatre and organise charity, since 'the impious Galilaeans support not only their own poor but ours as well'. He sacrificed hecatombs, wrote hymns to King Helios and the Mother of the Gods, and planned to rebuild the Jewish Temple at Jerusalem. At Antioch he removed the relics of the martyr Babylas from the sanctuary of Apollo at Daphne; when the temple burned on 22 October 362 he closed the cathedral in reprisal and was mocked by the Christian and frivolous Antiochenes, to whom he replied with the satirical Misopogon.

The programme lasted only eighteen months and collapsed with his death in June 363. Even sympathisers like Ammianus thought his sacrifices excessive and the school law unjust. Historians (Bowersock, Smith, Elm) see the restoration as revealing how far Christianity had already changed paganism, which Julian reimagined as a unified 'Hellenism' modelled partly on the church he hated.

scholarship: Bowersock, Julian the Apostate (1978)
Smith, Julian's Gods (1995)
Elm, Sons of Hellenism, Fathers of the Church (2012)

set.detail:
After failing to besiege Ctesiphon and burning his fleet, Julian led his army north along the left bank of the Tigris in June 363, harried by Persian cavalry and elephants and short of food, since the Persians had burned the crops. On 26 June, near a place Ammianus calls Phrygia and later writers Maranga or Samarra, the Persians attacked the rearguard. Julian, roused from his tent, rushed into the fight without putting on his breastplate. A cavalry spear grazed his arm and lodged in his liver; trying to pull it out he cut the tendons of his fingers and fell from his horse. He was carried to his tent, rallied briefly and asked for his weapons, then lay discussing the sublimity of the soul with the philosophers Maximus and Priscus, rebuked his weeping friends, and died around midnight, aged 31 or 32, after a reign of under two years as sole emperor.

Who threw the spear was immediately contested. Ammianus does not know. Libanius, in his funeral oration, insists that the killer was a Christian in the Roman army, since the Persians offered a reward and no one claimed it. Christian writers saw divine vengeance: Sozomen reports an unidentified horseman, later legend identified the martyr Mercurius sent by the Virgin, and Theodoret first records Julian's supposed dying words, throwing his blood to heaven, 'You have conquered, Galilaean'. Julian was buried at Tarsus, as he had wished; his tomb was later moved to Constantinople.

The death left the army trapped deep in Persian territory, without a commander or a successor. The officers chose Jovian, who made the humiliating peace of 363. Julian's death ended the last attempt to restore paganism as the religion of the state, and his memory divided late antiquity: hero of Libanius, Ammianus and Eunapius, archetypal apostate for Gregory of Nazianzus and the church.

scholarship: Bowersock, Julian the Apostate (1978)
Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)

set.detail:
Flavius Jovianus, the 32-year-old commander of the guard (primicerius domesticorum) and a Christian, was chosen emperor by the officers on 27 June 363 after the aged prefect Salutius refused. The army continued the retreat but was halted at Dura on the Tigris, unable to cross the river in flood, with only a few days of food left. Shapur, though his own army had suffered, sent his commander Surena with terms, and the Romans accepted after four days of negotiation, in early July 363.

The terms, preserved by Ammianus, Zosimus and Festus, were: a thirty-year peace; Rome returned the five Transtigritane regions won in 299 (Arzanene, Moxoene, Zabdicene, Rehimene and Corduene) with fifteen fortresses; Rome ceded Nisibis, Singara and Castra Maurorum, its strongest fortresses in Mesopotamia; and Rome undertook not to help its ally Arsaces of Armenia against Persia. Nisibis, which had resisted three Persian sieges, was handed over intact on condition that its inhabitants could leave: Ammianus describes the citizens begging Jovian to let them defend themselves, and their tearful departure, many moving to Amida and Edessa, including the poet-theologian Ephrem the Syrian.

Ammianus, who was with the army, calls the treaty shameful and unnecessary, claiming that the army could have reached the Roman province of Corduene in four days, and blames Jovian's haste to secure the throne. Eutropius notes that Romans had never before ceded territory, though they had made peace in difficult circumstances. Modern historians (Blockley, Lenski) are more understanding of Jovian's position. The treaty fixed the Roman-Persian frontier for a long period, made Nisibis a Persian stronghold and centre of Persian Christianity, and abandoned Armenia, leading to Shapur's capture of Arsaces and the Armenian wars of the 360s-370s.

scholarship: Blockley, "The Romano-Persian Peace Treaties of A.D. 299 and 363", Florilegium 6 (1984)
Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)

set.detail:
Jovian died suddenly at Dadastana on the border of Galatia and Bithynia on 17 February 364, from charcoal fumes or indigestion. The army's leading officers, meeting at Nicaea, considered several candidates; Salutius again declined. They chose Flavius Valentinianus, born in 321 at Cibalae in Pannonia, son of the general Gratian 'the Rope-maker', a tough, irascible officer and tribune of a schola of the guard, who was at Ancyra. Christian writers later claimed he had been dismissed by Julian for refusing to sacrifice. He was proclaimed on 26 February 364 at Nicaea. When the soldiers demanded that he name a colleague at once, he silenced them with a firm speech, but agreed to choose one. The magister equitum Dagalaifus advised: 'If you love your family, best of emperors, you have a brother; if you love the state, look for someone else to invest.'

Valentinian chose his brother. On 28 March 364, at the Hebdomon parade ground outside Constantinople, he made Flavius Valens, then 36 and a comparatively obscure officer, co-Augustus, though clearly subordinate. The brothers travelled west together and at Mediana near Naissus and then at Sirmium, in the summer of 364, divided the officials, palace staff and field army between them; Valentinian took the west with residence at Milan and then Trier, while Valens took the east, with Constantinople and Antioch. The division of the comitatus into regional armies was formalised in the process.

The partition of 364 was the most systematic since the Tetrarchy and anticipated the definitive division of 395. It made the two brothers effective in managing two frontiers, but it also exposed the east to Valens' weaknesses, from the revolt of Procopius in 365 to Adrianople in 378. Ammianus, books 26-31, is the main source and gives memorable portraits of both rulers.

scholarship: Lenski, Failure of Empire: Valens and the Roman State in the Fourth Century AD (2002)

set.detail:
In the early 370s the Huns, a nomadic people from the steppe, attacked the Alans east of the Don and then the Greuthungian Goths of Ermenaric, who, Ammianus says, killed himself; his successor Vithimir fell in battle, and the Greuthungi retreated under the regents Alatheus and Saphrax for the boy king Videric. The Huns next surprised Athanaric's Tervingi on the Dniester. Athanaric withdrew to the Carpathians and fortified a line, but most of the Tervingi, short of food and frightened, broke away under Alavivus and Fritigern and in 376 gathered on the north bank of the Danube, asking Valens, then at Antioch, to admit them to Thrace in return for military service.

Valens agreed, Ammianus says, because his flatterers convinced him that the newcomers would provide recruits and that provincials could pay their recruiting obligation in gold. The crossing, probably near Durostorum, took days and nights in boats, rafts and hollowed tree trunks, and many drowned. Eunapius claims 200,000 people crossed; modern estimates of the Tervingian warriors range from about 10,000 to 20,000, with their families. Roman officials were supposed to disarm them and separate the children as hostages, but the operation was mismanaged, and the Greuthungi and other groups crossed without permission when the guard was withdrawn.

The comes Lupicinus and the dux Maximus exploited the starving Goths, selling them dog meat at the price of one slave per dog, so that Gothic nobles sold their children. At Marcianople early in 377 Lupicinus tried to kill Fritigern and Alavivus at a banquet; Fritigern escaped, and the Goths rose in revolt, defeating Lupicinus. The ensuing war led to Adrianople. Ammianus compares the arrival of the barbarians to the ashes of Etna. Historians debate the numbers and the terms of reception (Heather, Lenski, Kulikowski), and Valens' motives, but agree that the admission of a whole people under its own leaders without adequate control was a turning point.

scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)

set.detail:
Valens returned from the east to Constantinople at the end of May 378, faced riots, and moved to Adrianople. His general Sebastianus had won small successes against Gothic raiding parties. Gratian, delayed by the Lentienses whom he defeated at Argentaria, sent Richomeres urging Valens to wait for him. Valens, perhaps jealous of his nephew's victory, held a council: Victor advised waiting, Sebastianus attacking, and scouts reported that Fritigern's force numbered only some 10,000. On 9 August 378 Valens left his baggage under guard at Adrianople and marched about eight Roman miles over rough ground in the summer heat, reaching the Gothic wagon laager about 2 p.m. with the troops tired, hungry and thirsty.

Fritigern, whose Greuthungian allies under Alatheus and Saphrax were away foraging, played for time by sending envoys, including a Christian priest, and offered peace in exchange for hostages; the Goths lit fires to blow smoke and heat over the Romans. As Richomeres was about to go as hostage, units of archers and scutarii under Bacurius and Cassio attacked without orders. At that moment the Greuthungian and Alan cavalry arrived 'like a thunderbolt' from the hills and struck the Roman left, which had pushed to the wagons and was isolated. The infantry was crowded so densely that the men could not draw their swords or raise their arms; the dust hid the sky. Two thirds of the army perished, including Sebastianus, Trajanus, 35 tribunes and many officers. Valens was killed; Ammianus records two versions, that he fell among the common soldiers, or that he was taken to a farmhouse which the Goths burned. His body was never found.

Ammianus says that no battle except Cannae had been so destructive. Modern estimates of the Roman army range from about 15,000 to 30,000. The Goths failed to take Adrianople and Constantinople, but the defeat led to Theodosius' appointment and the settlement of 382. Gibbon and later historians made it the beginning of the end of the western empire.
set.debate: Size of the armies (Ammianus gives no total) and exact site north of Adrianople disputed.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Burns, "The Battle of Adrianople: A Reconsideration", Historia 22 (1973)
Barbero, The Day of the Barbarians (2007)
Lenski, "Initium mali Romano imperio", TAPA 127 (1997)

set.detail:
Flavius Theodosius, born on 11 January 347 at Cauca in Gallaecia, was the son of the great general Count Theodosius, with whom he served in Britain and Africa. As dux of Moesia Prima in 374 he defeated the Sarmatians who had invaded after the murder of the Quadic king Gabinius. After his father's execution at Carthage early in 376, he retired to his estates in Spain. After Adrianople Gratian, now responsible for the whole empire, recalled him and appointed him magister militum; Theodoret claims Theodosius won a victory over Sarmatians before his elevation, which some scholars doubt.

On 19 January 379, at Sirmium, Gratian proclaimed Theodosius Augustus for the east, giving him the dioceses of Thrace and Oriens and the Illyrian dioceses of Dacia and Macedonia, temporarily, to conduct the Gothic war. Theodosius established himself at Thessalonica, rebuilt the shattered eastern army by recruiting widely, including peasants, miners, Goths and other barbarians, and by enforcing conscription. In 380 he was defeated in Macedonia when barbarian recruits deserted to Fritigern; he fell seriously ill at Thessalonica and was baptised by the Nicene bishop Acholius, which preceded his decisive religious legislation. Gratian's generals Bauto and Arbogast cleared Macedonia and Thessaly. Theodosius entered Constantinople on 24 November 380.

The appointment of a Spaniard with no dynastic link to the house of Valentinian, marrying later into it through Galla, established the Theodosian dynasty, which ruled the east until 457 and the west until 455. Historians (Errington, Sivan, McLynn) debate the circumstances of the proclamation: whether Gratian acted freely or under pressure from the army and the Spanish faction at court, and whether the reports of a preliminary Sarmatian victory were later invention to legitimise the choice.

scholarship: Errington, Roman Imperial Policy from Julian to Theodosius (2006)
Sivan, "Was Theodosius I a Usurper?", Klio 78 (1996)

set.detail:
On 27 February 380, from Thessalonica, Theodosius, together with his colleagues Gratian and Valentinian II, issued a law addressed 'to the people of the city of Constantinople', preserved in the Theodosian Code (16.1.2) and later placed at the head of Justinian's Code. Its opening words, 'Cunctos populos', declare: 'It is our will that all the peoples ruled by the administration of our clemency shall practise that religion which the divine apostle Peter transmitted to the Romans, as the religion which he introduced makes clear even to this day. It is evident that this is the religion followed by the pontiff Damasus and by Peter, bishop of Alexandria, a man of apostolic holiness; that is, according to apostolic discipline and evangelic doctrine, we shall believe in the single deity of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, in equal majesty and in a holy Trinity.' Those who followed this law were to be called Catholic Christians; the rest, 'demented and insane', were to bear the infamy of heretical dogma, and their meeting places would not be called churches; they would be punished first by divine vengeance and then by imperial action.

The law was issued while Constantinople was still controlled by the Homoian bishop Demophilus and before Theodosius had entered the city. After his baptism, in November 380 he expelled Demophilus and installed Gregory of Nazianzus, and on 10 January 381 a further law (CTh 16.5.6) handed all churches to Nicene bishops. The council of Constantinople then defined orthodoxy in synodal form.

Often described as making Christianity the state religion of the empire, the edict was in fact a definition of orthodox Christianity, addressed primarily to the capital, and its immediate targets were Homoian and other Christian groups rather than pagans. Malcolm Errington argues that its scope was limited and that imperial religious policy remained cautious; but it set the precedent for a long series of laws enforcing a single imperial orthodoxy.

scholarship: Errington, "Christian Accounts of the Religious Legislation of Theodosius I", Klio 79 (1997)
McLynn, Ambrose of Milan (1994)

set.detail:
Theodosius summoned eastern bishops to Constantinople in May 381 to confirm the Nicene settlement and fill the see of the capital. About 150 bishops of the Nicene party attended, together with 36 'Macedonians' (Pneumatomachi, who denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit), who walked out when they refused to accept the Nicene faith. Meletius of Antioch presided until his death during the council, followed by a solemn funeral with an oration by Gregory of Nyssa. Gregory of Nazianzus was confirmed as bishop of Constantinople and presided, but, attacked by the Egyptian and Macedonian bishops over his transfer from Sasima and frustrated by the decision to continue the Antiochene schism, he resigned in a farewell sermon. He was replaced by Nectarius, an elderly unbaptised senator and former praetor, who was baptised, ordained and consecrated within days.

The council's first canon confirmed the faith of Nicaea and anathematised every heresy: Eunomians or Anomoeans, Arians or Eudoxians, Semi-Arians or Pneumatomachi, Sabellians, Marcellians, Photinians and Apollinarians. Canon 2 forbade bishops to interfere outside their own dioceses, and canon 3 declared that 'the bishop of Constantinople shall have the primacy of honour after the bishop of Rome, because it is New Rome', which offended both Rome and Alexandria. The creed now recited in most churches as the 'Nicene Creed', with its expanded article on the Spirit, 'the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified', was attributed to this council by the council of Chalcedon in 451; whether it was actually issued in 381 is debated.

A law of 30 July 381 (CTh 16.1.3) named the bishops with whom communion defined orthodoxy. The council marked the end of the Arian controversy within the empire, though not among the Goths, and was accepted as the second ecumenical council in 451.

scholarship: Ritter, Das Konzil von Konstantinopel und sein Symbol (1965)
Kelly, Early Christian Creeds (3rd ed., 1972)

set.detail:
After Adrianople the Goths could not be defeated in the field, nor take walled cities. Theodosius, rebuilding the eastern army, and Gratian's generals waged a war of attrition in 379-381; in 380 Gratian settled the Greuthungi of Alatheus and Saphrax in Pannonia, and Athanaric died in Constantinople in January 381. On 3 October 382, according to the Consularia Constantinopolitana, 'the entire people of the Goths with their king surrendered to the Roman empire'. The agreement was negotiated by the magister militum Saturninus, whom Themistius praised in an oration for the consulship of 383.

The terms are known only indirectly, from Themistius, Pacatus, Synesius and later writers. The Goths (mainly Tervingi, with others) received land in the diocese of Thrace, between the Danube and the Balkan mountains and in Dacia Ripensis and Moesia, which they farmed, probably free of tax. They remained a distinct people under their own leaders rather than being dispersed and placed under Roman officials, and they were obliged to provide soldiers who fought in their own units under their own commanders when the emperor called them, receiving subsidies. Themistius argued that it was better to fill Thrace with farmers than with corpses, and that the Goths would one day become Romans as the Galatians had.

Modern historians debate how revolutionary the treaty was. Peter Heather sees the Goths as a semi-autonomous people within the empire for the first time, a step towards the barbarian kingdoms of the fifth century. Others (Errington, Liebeschuetz) argue that its terms resembled traditional settlements and that the Goths' autonomy grew only later. In any case, Gothic federates fought for Theodosius against Maximus (388) and Eugenius (394), and the heavy losses at the Frigidus helped provoke the revolt of Alaric in 395.

scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)
Errington, "Theodosius and the Goths", Chiron 26 (1996)

set.detail:
Magnus Maximus, a Spaniard from Gallaecia and probably a relative of Theodosius, had served under Count Theodosius in Britain in 368-369 and Africa in 373-374 and held a command in Britain, where in 382 he defeated the Picts and Scots. In the spring of 383 the British army proclaimed him emperor. Its grievances against Gratian were his neglect of the west, his favour for the Alan bodyguard whose dress he adopted, and his reliance on Milanese and Frankish advisers. Maximus crossed to Gaul with much of the British garrison.

Gratian met him near Paris, but after five days of skirmishes his army, starting with Moorish cavalry, deserted. He fled south with a few horsemen and was caught at Lugdunum by Maximus' magister equitum Andragathius, who killed him on 25 August 383. Maximus established his court at Trier, made his son Victor co-Augustus and controlled Britain, Gaul and Spain. Theodosius, busy in the east, recognised him for several years; his statues were set up even in Alexandria. Ambrose went to Trier twice on behalf of the boy Valentinian II and his mother Justina in Milan. Maximus presented himself as a champion of Nicene orthodoxy, and at the instigation of Spanish bishops he had the ascetic Priscillian and his followers tried and executed at Trier in 385, the first execution of Christians for heresy, despite the protests of Martin of Tours and Ambrose.

In 387 Maximus invaded Italy; Valentinian fled to Theodosius, who in 388 defeated Maximus at Siscia and Poetovio and executed him at Aquileia. Gildas later blamed Maximus for stripping Britain of its soldiers, and Welsh tradition remembered him as Macsen Wledig, husband of Elen, ancestor of Welsh dynasties and founder of Brittany through Conan Meriadoc, in the medieval tale The Dream of Macsen Wledig.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Matthews, Western Aristocracies and Imperial Court AD 364-425 (1975)
Birley, The Roman Government of Britain (2005)

set.detail:
In 390 Butheric, the Gothic magister militum per Illyricum stationed at Thessalonica, imprisoned a popular charioteer who, according to Sozomen, had attempted to seduce or assault a male servant (or Butheric himself, in some readings). When the charioteer's absence threatened the races, the people demanded his release, and when Butheric refused, they rioted and killed him and several officers. Theodosius, then in Milan, angered by the murder of a senior commander and perhaps influenced by advisers such as Rufinus, ordered a punitive response. He later countermanded the order, but too late. The people were invited to the races; soldiers closed the exits of the hippodrome and massacred the spectators for hours. Theodoret puts the dead at 7,000; Rufinus gives no number.

Ambrose, who had been excluded from the emperor's councils about the affair, withdrew from Milan and wrote Theodosius a private letter, preserved outside the main collection, urging him to do penance and declaring that he would not offer the sacrifice in his presence. Theodosius performed public penance, laying aside his imperial insignia, and was readmitted to communion, probably at Christmas 390. In his funeral oration for Theodosius in 395, Ambrose praised his humility. Theodoret's later dramatic version, in which Ambrose stopped the emperor at the door of the cathedral, is unhistorical. A law requiring a thirty-day delay before execution of sentences of death or confiscation (CTh 9.40.13) has been linked to the episode, though its date is uncertain.

The episode became a medieval and early modern exemplar of the church's moral authority over secular rulers. Neil McLynn and others interpret the penance as a carefully managed act that allowed Theodosius to restore his reputation and re-establish his relationship with the powerful bishop after the Callinicum affair, rather than a humiliation imposed by Ambrose.
set.debate: Number of victims (Theodoret 7,000); date (spring or summer 390); nature of the penance.

scholarship: McLynn, Ambrose of Milan: Church and Court in a Christian Capital (1994)
Kolb, "Der Bussakt von Mailand", in Geschichte und Gegenwart (1980)

set.detail:
The Serapeum of Alexandria, built under Ptolemy III and rebuilt under the Romans, stood on a hill in the Rhakotis quarter: a vast precinct with porticoes, a daughter library of the Museum and a colossal statue of Serapis attributed to Bryaxis, made of wood covered in precious metals and jewels. On 24 February 391 a law of Theodosius to the prefect of Rome (CTh 16.10.10) banned sacrifice and visits to temples; on 16 June a similar law (16.10.11) was sent to the Augustal prefect Evagrius and the comes Romanus in Egypt.

In Alexandria Bishop Theophilus obtained a disused temple (a Mithraeum or temple of Dionysus) to turn into a church and paraded its cult objects in mockery. Pagans, led by the philosopher Olympius, rioted, killed Christians and barricaded themselves in the Serapeum with Christian hostages, some of whom they crucified or forced to sacrifice. The officials referred the matter to the emperor, whose reply pardoned the pagans, making the Christian dead martyrs, but ordered the temples destroyed. When the letter was read, the pagans fled. Rufinus, who arrived in Alexandria soon after, describes how a soldier struck the face of the Serapis statue with an axe, mice ran out of the head, and its pieces were dragged through the city and burned. The temple was demolished and a church and martyr shrine, later dedicated to John the Baptist, built on the site.

The destruction was the most spectacular episode of the end of paganism, celebrated by Christians and mourned by Eunapius. Some modern writers have linked it with the destruction of the Library of Alexandria, but the Serapeum's book collection had probably dwindled by then. The date (391 or 392) and the relation to imperial law are debated (Hahn, Watts). The Nile cubit used to measure the flood was moved from the Serapeum to a church.

scholarship: Hahn, Gewalt und religiöser Konflikt (2004)
Watts, Riot in Alexandria (2010)
McKenzie et al., "Reconstructing the Serapeum in Alexandria", JRS 94 (2004)

set.detail:
After the death of Valentinian II at Vienne in May 392, the Frankish magister militum Arbogast proclaimed the rhetor Flavius Eugenius emperor in August 392. Theodosius refused recognition, made his son Honorius Augustus in January 393, and in 394 marched west with an army including some 20,000 Gothic federates under Gainas, Alaric and Saul, the Iberian prince Bacurius, and his generals Stilicho and Timasius. Eugenius' regime, dominated by the pagan prefect Nicomachus Flavianus, set up statues of Jupiter in the Alps and carried images of Hercules on its standards.

Theodosius crossed the Julian Alps unopposed and on 5 September 394 found Eugenius' army waiting on the river Frigidus (the Vipava, in modern Slovenia) near Castra (Ajdovščina). On the first day he sent his Goths in against the enemy positions; they suffered heavy losses, perhaps 10,000 according to Orosius, and Bacurius was killed. Eugenius' men celebrated. During the night Arbogast sent a force to occupy the passes behind Theodosius, but its commander Arbitio defected. On 6 September Theodosius attacked again. A violent wind, the bora that blows down the Vipava valley, rose and blew dust into the faces of Eugenius' army and turned their missiles back on them, as Claudian, Ambrose, Orosius, Socrates and others all report, with Christian writers presenting it as an answer to Theodosius' prayers. Eugenius' army broke; Eugenius was captured and beheaded, Arbogast fled into the mountains and killed himself, and Flavianus also committed suicide. Augustine tells that Theodosius' soldiers jokingly asked to be struck by the golden thunderbolts of the captured Jupiter statues.

Theodosius became sole ruler but died at Milan on 17 January 395. The battle is often presented as the final defeat of paganism; Alan Cameron argues its religious character was exaggerated by Christian writers. The heavy Gothic losses fuelled the resentment behind Alaric's revolt in 395.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans
Panegyric on the Third Consulship of Honorius

scholarship: Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
